games, and the Pittsburgh percentage
on the pennant chances exchange has
been lowered from .600 to .550. The
Cardinals were boosted some points this
week, from .475 to .520.

O'Farrell's catching has been nothing
short of amazing. Alexander,
Sherdel, Haines and Ehmke have
pitched unhittable and unbeatable
ball. Haines heretofore has never
been considered as much of a Spring
pitcher, but he has been wow so far.
Ehmke jumped in without any train-
ing and is getting off to as good a
start as in 1926.

THE Pirates suffered their first real
blow in St. Louis, and it was a blow
to the Pirate morale as much as any
thing else. Two of the Pittsburgh
twirling aces, Aldridge and Kremer,
held the Cards to three runs in two
games, but the Buccaneers lost both.
Aldridge beat the former, 2 to 1, and
Haines beat Kremer, 1 to 0. Those
were hard defeats for Joe Bush to
take, and his club has been floundering
more or less ever since.

Still Favors Pirates.

The only apprehension felt about the
Pirates has been in the pitching de-
partment. I would not admit that the
Pirate pitching was as bad as some
would paint it. However, so far the
club's pitching staff has consisted
largely of Kremer and Meadows. The
spectacled Carmen Hill has failed to
show the expected improvement and
Joe Bush's arm apparently is through.
But Pittsburgh has strong offensive
power and the Pirates still are my
favorites.

In the first 10 days of the race
the Giants did not look any too good,
but recently they have taken full ad-
vantage of the soft picking in the
East. And as my co-worker, John
McGraw, pointed out the other day,
pennants are won on the victories
which are hammered down the throats
of the second division teams. As
a rule the contenders come very close
to breaking even.

Hornsby continues to hit in his
best form. Judging from his early
start, he is due for another 400 bat-
ting average, and he has been a big
factor in New York's recent run of
victories.

Reds Counted Out.

The Cubs, my National League
dark horses again, are going a little
better, but it doesn't look now as
though McCarthy will have as formid-
able a team as he did last year. Cin-
cinnati already has shown enough to
convince even its most loyal hackers
that the club will not be a contender
as it was a year ago.

Darcy Flowers should brace up the
weakened Dodger infield, but he is
only an average player, and Brooklyn
needs a new team outside of the bat-
teries. The Phillies continue to hold
up, and with Carlson, Scott, Ferguson
and Pruett going fairly well, they
should put up a fight for the top of
the National League's second division.
The Braves already have blown up.

As I now see the National League
race, it looks like Pittsburgh, St.
Louis and New York fighting it out
for the pennant, a big gap in the mid-
dle, and then Chicago, Cincinnati,
Philadelphia, Boston and Brooklyn on
the other end of the procession.
In the American League my dope
is coming out pretty well. I placed
the Athletics and Yankees in group I,
with the Tigers the outside contender.
After going through their first four
game series at Yankee Stadium with-
out winning a game, the Athletics
have braced up and now are right up
with the American League champions.

Come to Life.

However, I am surprised at the
weak pitching of the Athletics. There
is scarcely a game in which Connie
Mack gets by with his starting pitcher.
Eddie Rommel has been almost use-
less so far, and Ehmke has not per-
formed up to expectations. Hard hit-
ting, which has overcome a lot of big
leads, has given the club its victories.
And Cobb, the 40-year-old gladiator,
has been in almost every Philadelphia
rally.

Huggins' pitching staff was pretty
well knocked to pieces last week, and
just as little Miller was in a quandary
as to who he would pitch, a lot of
rain and cold descended on New York,
and the Yankees put in three days
toasting their toes. That gave Ruether
a chance to recover from a wrenched
side, Hoyt to regain his strength after
cold, and Pennock few more days
to get over an injury to his foot.

Babe Ruth's batting start has not
been as impressive as that of Rogers
Hornsby on the Giants, but I think
this talk about Ruth having "Klein
eyes" is a lot of bunk. The Babe will
be right up with the leading hitters
in another week.

Griffs Need Johnson.

The American League brand of
pitching seems to be pretty poor all
along the line. Washington has 13
pitchers, but many of them are little
more than names on the score card.
Thurston, former White Sox, won a
well pitched game for Bucky Harris,
but lately he, too, has been taking his
bumps. They need old Walter John-
son for the anchor man of the staff.
Walter is about ready to resume firing,
and he is needed.

Ray Schalk is getting about as good
pitching as any manager in the league,
and his team is giving a splendid ac-
count of itself. Old Roger Peckin-
paugh has been benched, and Bill
Kneifel is now playing shortstop
and hitting well. Aaron Ward, the
corner Yankee, is hitting down with
the pitchers.

Big George Uhle is doing little for
the Indians this Spring, and Cleveland
is getting off to an uncertain start.
